title: Rock Layers and Fossils
seo_title: Grade 4 Rock Layers and Fossils Worksheets: Oldest Layers and Changing Landscapes
standard_text: Identify evidence from patterns in rock formations and fossils in rock layers to support an explanation for changes in a landscape over time.
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 science worksheets on rock layers and fossils (NGSS 4-ESS1-1): oldest and youngest layers, what fossils show about past environments, and how canyons form over time. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: In rock layers, the bottom layer is the oldest.
key_sub: Fossils in each layer show what the area was like long ago, like ocean (seashells) or land (ferns).
body_html:
How to think about it

Rock layers form one on top of another, so in layers that have not been turned over, the bottom layer is the oldest and the top layer is the youngest.

Fossils in the layers tell us what the area was like when each layer formed: seashells and fish mean it was under water; ferns and footprints mean it was land.

A canyon shows that a river cut down through the layers over a very long time.

Example

A fish fossil is in a lower layer and a leaf fossil is in a higher layer. How did the area change?

Lower layers are older.

Fish → water; leaf → land.

Answer: It was under water, then it became land.

Example

Which layer of a canyon wall is the oldest?

Layers form from the bottom up.

Answer: the bottom layer

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the top layer is the oldest.
  • Thinking a sea fossil means the area is ocean today. It tells about the past.
  • Thinking canyons form quickly. They take a very long time.

faq.q: Which rock layer is the oldest?
faq.a: In layers that have not been turned over, the bottom layer is the oldest because each new layer forms on top.
They show what lived in an area long ago, so they tell us whether the area was ocean, a lake or dry land.

faq.q: Why are there seashell fossils on mountains?
faq.a: The rock formed under the ocean long ago and was slowly pushed up to form the mountains.
